component_findings.async_structured: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Asynchronous concurrency has first-class composition and structured lifetime/join/cancellation mechanisms or an equivalent disciplined model. Evidence basis: Static language-design analysis of TypeScript's concurrency model (single-threaded event loop, async/await, Promises, Worker Threads) based on language semantics and inspection of readable micro-benchmark sources. | TypeScript inherits JavaScript's single-threaded, event-loop-based concurrency model. There is no shared-memory multithreading in the language itself; true parallelism requires spawning separate Worker Threads (or Web Workers) with message-passing (structured clone / SharedArrayBuffer for shared memory). | async/await and Promises are first-class, well-integrated language/type-system features (Promise<T> is fully generic-typed), giving excellent ergonomics for I/O-bound concurrency and composing asynchronous pipelines with strong static typing of resolved values and errors. | No built-in structured concurrency or cancellation beyond library convention; AbortController is a runtime pattern layered on top, not enforced by the type system. | CPU-bound parallelism is comparatively weak: Worker Threads require explicit message-passing boilerplate, structured cloning overhead, and separate module loading, unlike native shared-memory threads with typed channels (Rust, Go, Java, Kotlin). | SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics exist for low-level shared-memory concurrency across workers but are unergonomic, unsafe (no compiler-enforced data-race protection), and rarely idiomatic in t…

component_findings.abi_calling_control: Recertified level 1 under the current criterion: ABI/calling-convention/linkage choices are explicit or safely standardized for common interoperability cases. Evidence basis: Static language-design analysis of TypeScript/JavaScript FFI model on Node.js runtime, informed by inspection of readable TypeScript micro-benchmark sources under template/programs/typescript/micro. | TypeScript itself has no native FFI keyword or ABI-level interop; interop is delegated entirely to the underlying JS runtime (Node.js N-API/node-ffi, Deno FFI, or WASM bindings). | Calling native code requires either writing a native Node addon in C/C++ using N-API (a separate compiled artifact, not part of TS language semantics) or using a third-party FFI package (e.g. ffi-napi, koffi) that maps C signatures dynamically at runtime with no compile-time type checking against the native side. | TypeScript's structural type system and .d.ts declaration files give reasonable static typing quality for JS-side wrappers once a hand-written or generated .d.ts exists, but the FFI boundary itself is untyped/unsafe (raw pointers as opaque numbers/BigInt, manual marshalling of structs/buffers). | WebAssembly interop (via Emscripten or wasm-bindgen-style tooling) is ergonomically decent but still requires generated glue and is not a language-level construct. | No first-class syntax for calling into shared libraries directly (unlike Zig's @cImport or Go's cgo); all approaches go through the host runtime's C++ embedding API or third-party packages. | Async/Promise-based native call wrapping is i…
